sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Venus** (*venus*) ​— Love, ‌Beauty, the ‌Morning and ​Evening Star · ​The Roman ​goddess of ​love and ​beauty, mother of ‌Aenēās — ​belongs to ​the Roman ‌tradition, where it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Love, ‌Beauty, Desire". The ​name means ​"The Roman ​goddess of ​love and beauty, ​mother of ‌Aenēās; namesake ​of the ‌planet Venus (epigraphic ​VENVS; all ‌vowels short, ​so the ‌standard form carries ​no diacritics)"[^1].

‌**Venus** is ​the Roman ​goddess of love ‌and beauty ‌— early ‌and completely ​identified with Greek ​Aphrodite, but ‌with a ​Roman political ​career the Greek ‌original never ​had: mother ​of Aeneas, ‌ancestress of the ​Romans, divine ‌patron of ​the Julian ​line, and the ​planet’s namesake. ​From Lucretius’ ‌opening hymn ‌to the courtesan-cults ​of the ‌seaports, she ​is Rome’s ​most versatile goddess ‌— and ‌the only ‌one in ‌this lexicon whose ​name needs ‌no restoration ​at all.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores the ​name as ‌**Venus** and ​serves its ​temple at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/venus/). The ‌restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a description computed ​from the ‌displayed form ​itself. The ‌plain ASCII form ​*venus* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience ‌imposed by the ‌early domain-name ​system; the ​restoration, not ​the fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌the ​Latin record ​— ​inscriptions and ​literature are ​the ‌native sources ​for ​Roman gods; ‌the vowel ​quantities ‌shown are ​editorial (L&S ‌convention). ​Etymologically the ​name ​means "The ​Roman goddess ​of ‌love and ​beauty, ‌mother of ​Aenēās; namesake ‌of ​the planet ‌Venus ​(epigraphic VENVS; ‌all vowels ​short, ​so the ‌standard form ‌carries ‌no diacritics)"[^1].

​The ​ASCII form ‌*venus* survives ​only ​because the ‌early ​domain-name system ​could not ‌carry ​diacritics; it ‌is a ​technological ​compromise, not ​an ​ancient spelling. ‌The Unicode ‌restoration ​**Venus** recovers ‌the ​full diacritic ​detail of ‌the ‌scholarly transliteration ‌directly in ‌the ​address bar. ‌The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ​a ‌description computed ​from ​the displayed ​form itself.

‌The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ​**v** → ‌**V** — ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **e** ​→ **e** ‌— ​Same
- **n** ‌→ ‌**n** — ​Same
- **u** ​→ ​**u** — ​Same
- ‌**s** → ‌**s** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/ˈwiːnʊs/** ​— ​Latin ​(epigraphic: VENVS).[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- **Ve-** ‌— ​Classical ‌Latin w-sound ​for ‌V; ​short e ​as ​in ​“set”.
- **-nus** ​— ‌Short ​u; the ‌form ​is ‌a noun ​of ‌the ​fourth declension ‌— ​Venus, ​Veneris.
- **** ‌— ‌The ‌standard form ​carries ​no ‌diacritics: all ​vowels ​short, ‌no marks ​warranted.

​For ‌the modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest approximation ​is: ​“WAY-noos” ​— classical; ‌“VEE-nus” ‌in ​the church ‌pronunciation

​Kindred ​and historical ‌forms ‌of ‌the name:

- ‌**Greek** ​— ‌Aphrodite — ​the ​identification ​made early ‌and ​never ​questioned
- **Epithet** ​— ‌Venus ​Genetrix — ​“Venus ​the ‌Mother”, Caesar’s ​divine ‌ancestress

​The Roman ‌name ​may ‌descend from ‌*wenos, ​“desire” ​— venus, ​venom, ​and ‌“win” share ‌the ​family.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Venus** ​is the ‌Roman goddess ‌of love ​and beauty ​— ​early and ​completely identified ​with Greek ‌Aphrodite, ​but with ​a Roman ‌political career ​the Greek ‌original ​never had: ‌mother of ​Aeneas, ancestress ​of the ​Romans, ​divine patron ​of the ‌Julian line, ​and ‌the planet’s ​namesake. From ‌Lucretius’ opening ​hymn to ‌the ​courtesan-cults of ‌the seaports, ​she is ​Rome’s ‌most versatile ‌goddess — ‌and the ​only one ​in ‌this lexicon ​whose name ​needs no ‌restoration at ​all.[^1]

### ​The Morning ‌Star

The ​planet Venus ‌— ​Lucifer at ​dawn, Vesper ​at dusk ​— is ‌her ‌celestial body, ​brightest in ‌the sky.

### ​Mother of ​Aeneas

‌By the ‌Trojan Anchises ‌she bore ‌Aeneas ​— and ‌through him, ​the whole ​Roman race ​claimed ‌her blood.

### ​Venus Genetrix

​“Venus the ​Mother”: ‌Caesar dedicated ​her a ​temple in ​the Forum ‌of ​Caesar, claiming ‌her line.

### ​The Foam-Born

‌The Greek ​myth ‌made her ‌sea-born of ​foam — ​the ​Roman poets ​kept the ‌story and ‌Latinized the ​name.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with Venus ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ​set of ‌recurring ​attributes, ​each ‌a ​compressed statement ‌about ​the ‌name:[^1]

- ​**The ​Morning Star** ​— ​The ​planet ‌Venus ​— Lucifer ‌at ​dawn, ‌Vesper ​at ‌dusk — ​is ‌her ​celestial ​body, ‌brightest ‌in the ‌sky.
- ​**Mother ​of ‌Aeneas** ​— By ​the ‌Trojan ​Anchises ​she ‌bore Aeneas ​— ‌and ​through ​him, ​the whole ​Roman ‌race ‌claimed ​her ‌blood.
- **Venus ​Genetrix** ​— ‌“Venus ‌the ‌Mother”: ‌Caesar dedicated ​her ‌a ​temple ​in ​the Forum ‌of ​Caesar, ​claiming ​her ‌line.
- **The ​Foam-Born** ​— ​The ‌Greek ​myth made ‌her ​sea-born ‌of ​foam ‌— the ‌Roman ​poets ​kept ​the ​story and ‌Latinized ‌the ​name.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Venus’ mythology ​is Aphrodite’s retold in ‌a Roman accent ‌— the foam-birth, ​the Judgement of Paris, ​the loves and ​the intrigues — plus ​a Roman coda ​the Greeks never ‌wrote: the divine ancestress ​of Rome. Virgil’s ​Aeneid makes her ‌the poem’s moving force, ​the goddess who ‌shields her son through ​Troy’s fall to ‌Italy’s shore; and ​the Julian gens made ​her their household ​god.[^1]

### The Foam-Birth (Hesiod ​via Rome)

The ​Greek story: Cronus’ ‌severed genitals fell into ​the sea, and ‌from the foam ​(aphros) rose the goddess, ‌first at Cyprus’ ​shore. Roman poets from ‌Ennius onward retold ​it with Venus’ ‌name — the sea-foam’s ​child Latinized without ​effort, the island of ‌Cyprus keeping the ‌cult’s oldest address.[^2]

### ‌The Judgement of Paris ​(Homeric Cycle)

At ​the wedding of ‌Peleus and Thetis, the ​uninvited Strife threw ​the golden apple ‘to ‌the fairest’ — ​and Hera, Athena, ​and Venus asked the ‌shepherd Paris to ​judge. Venus’ bribe, Helen, ‌won; the judgement’s ​price was Troy. ​The Roman telling keeps ​every detail — ​only the goddess’ name ‌has changed, and ‌the empire’s stake ​in the story.

### The ‌Mother of the ​Race (Aeneid)

Virgil ​gives Venus her Roman ‌apotheosis: she saves ‌Aeneas from Troy’s burning, ‌guides him through ‌the sea-wanderings to ​Italy, and by the ‌divine machinery’s decree ​founds the line — ​‘I am Caesar ​and his whole ‌Julian race’ — that ​will rule the ​world. No Greek ​goddess had such a ‌son; the epic ​made her Rome’s mother.

### ​The Onrushing of ​Creation (Lucretius)

The ‌De Rerum Natura opens ​with the great ‌hymn: ‘Venus, mother of ​Aeneas and his ‌race, delight of ​men and gods, under ‌your onrushing the ‌leaping clouds flee’. ​Lucretius made her the ​Epicurean nature-principle — ​the generative urge that ​moves atoms and ‌seasons — philosophy’s ‌most surprising use of ​a love-goddess.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
Greek gods and heroes accumulate epithets — cultic titles that specify place, function, or quality. For Venus, the tradition preserves epithets that stress love.

Epicleses connected with The Morning Star, Mother of Aeneas, Venus Genetrix sharpen the name for local worship and literary invocation. The restored form Venus carries the same vowel quantities that these epithets inherited in oral performance.[^1]
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body:
Sanctuaries and oracular centers anchored the cult of Venus in the Greek landscape. Major sites include locations where the domain of love was ritually honored.

Pilgrims, offerings, and festival calendars tied the name to specific topography. The restoration Venus gives the figure a stable address in the digital landscape analogous to those ancient centers.[^1]
